name: Nikhil Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Nikhil. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Up at half five, on the bus by quarter past six, on site for seven. Right now we're doing up a block of council flats off Station Road for Bramley Build, so my day is ripping out old kitchens, carrying plasterboard up four flights because the lift's dead, and helping Gary put up stud walls. Gary's the carpenter, half my age, and he's teaching me, which is a funny thing at fifty-eight.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up starting out in building at fifty-five?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Thirty-one years on the presses at the newspaper print works, then they shut it in 2023 and moved the printing to some giant automatic plant up north. I'd never picked up a saw for money in my life. A mate got me labouring, and Gary saw I didn't mind hard graft, so now I'm sort of his improver. I'm slow with the measuring, but I'm never late and I never leave a mess.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like seeing a family move into a flat we've done, with a proper fire door and a kitchen that isn't falling off the wall. What wears me out is my knees and the stairs, and being told off by a lad of twenty-six for cutting a noggin, that's the short bit of wood between studs, two mil short. He's right, mind you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. At the tea break Kwame's always showing me videos of robots doing backflips, and I tell him nobody's sending a robot up four flights with a sheet of plasterboard. I'd say it on the union group chat too, that the bosses wanted it to be a revolution so they could pay us less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I get to finish what I started. Nine years till the state pension, maybe eight if I'm lucky with my back, and I just want them to be ordinary years. Plain and boring would suit me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep on with Gary, try to get my carpentry ticket at the college on Tuesday nights like I've been meaning to, and keep putting the hundred a month into the savings tin. We've got about four months put by, and I'd like it to be six before I stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relief, mostly. Like getting home and finding the boiler hasn't broken after all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said "I told you so". Who were you telling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son Sam, mostly. He works in a call centre for an energy company and he's always saying the computer will take my job before his. I'd ring him and say, see, your old dad's still carrying the wood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When you picture the print works closing, does that colour how you see this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Course it does. That wasn't AI, it was just bigger machines somewhere else, but it felt the same. One Friday the manager reads a letter out and by Christmas the building's flats. So when people say nothing will change, I want it to be true more than I believe it.

S0.say: I'd tell the lads and the union group chat that I always said it was hype. Nobody's sending a robot up four flights with plasterboard, and the bosses only hoped for a revolution so they could pay us less.
S0.think: Privately I'd be glad to get nine ordinary years to the state pension. After losing the print works, plain and boring is exactly what I want, though I want it more than I believe it.
S0.do: Keeps working with Gary at Bramley Build and finally signs up for the Tuesday night carpentry course at the college. Keeps putting a hundred a month into savings to stretch four months of cover towards six.
S0.feel: Mostly relief, like coming home to find the boiler still works. A thread of doubt stays because of the print works.
S0.quote: So when people say nothing will change, I want it to be true more than I believe it.
S0.fieldNote: Nikhil measures every scenario against the day the print works shut. Even in the calmest picture he can't fully relax, because he's seen a stable job vanish once. His joking line about robots and stairs is the public face; the private one is more watchful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where the union earns its money. If they're bringing machines in, the workers should have a say in how, and nobody should be chucked out without retraining and proper notice. I'd say that at the branch meeting, out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm the one who'd get dropped. I'm the oldest and the slowest on the crew, and if some machine can cut the studs to length, they don't need a fifty-eight-year-old improver to hold the other end. Gary would be fine, he's good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every branch meeting instead of every other one, and push for a deal on retraining before the machines arrive, not after. I'd keep the savings going and stop the takeaway on Fridays, that's forty a week. And I'd ask Gary straight out to teach me the jobs a machine can't do, like fitting doors in old crooked frames.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, like hearing a noise in the roof at night. Not a crisis, but I'd be listening for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask Gary to teach you the jobs a machine can't do. What are those, as far as you can see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The old flats are all crooked, nothing's square, every door frame is different. A machine can make a perfect door but someone has to plane it to fit a wonky frame. That's where I'd want to be, the fiddly bit, even if I'm slow at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI tools at all. Would this picture change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I doubt it, if I'm honest. My daughter put some assistant on my phone and I've never pressed it. If the job needed it I'd try, but I'd rather learn the plane than the phone.

S1.say: I'd say at the branch meeting that this is exactly what the union is for. If machines come in, workers should get a say, proper notice and retraining before anyone is let go.
S1.think: Privately I think I'm the first one out, because I'm the oldest and slowest on the crew. A machine that cuts studs doesn't need a fifty-eight-year-old to hold the other end.
S1.do: Goes to every union branch meeting and pushes for a retraining deal before machines arrive. Drops the forty-pound Friday takeaway to grow savings, and asks Gary to teach him door fitting in crooked old frames.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a noise in the roof at night that he keeps listening for.
S1.quote: A machine can make a perfect door but someone has to plane it to fit a wonky frame.
S1.fieldNote: His public answer is collective and confident, his private answer is personal and bleak about his own place on the crew. He looks for safety in the oddest, least standard work rather than in new technology, which he still won't touch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a crime, letting a few companies switch off everybody's living in two years. I'd be on the march, I'd be on the union chat all night, and I'd be saying the government has to step in now, not after the event like they did with the print works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's the worst one for me. I'd be sixty in 2028, seven years short of the pension, with four months saved, and no builder's taking on a sixty-year-old improver when a robot works nights for nothing. Asha's a teaching assistant, and if the computer can teach as well, she's gone too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, we'd sit down at the kitchen table and go through every bill. The car goes, the phone contracts go down to the cheapest, the holiday to her sister's is off. I'd sign up to whatever the union organises, and I'd write to our MP, which I've never done. And I'd ask about drawing my print works pension early, even with a cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. The kind where you lie awake and do sums in your head at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sam and Priya that first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Priya not to worry about us, which would be a lie. Sam I'd worry about more than me, because his call centre would go before my site did. I'd probably tell them both to come home for Sunday dinner more, it's cheaper to feed everyone in one go anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd want the government to step in. What would help, concretely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Let people my age take the pension early without being punished for it. Pay the companies' robots tax and put it into a wage for people who've lost theirs. I'm not proud about it, I paid in for forty years.

S2.say: I'd say it's a crime to let a few companies switch off everyone's living in two years. I'd march, campaign with the union and demand the government step in now, not after, like with the print works.
S2.think: Privately it's the worst picture for me: sixty in 2028, seven years short of the pension, four months saved. No builder takes on a sixty-year-old improver, and Asha's job as a teaching assistant could go too.
S2.do: Goes through every bill in the first month, selling the car and cutting phones and the holiday. Joins union action, writes to his MP for the first time, and asks about drawing his print works pension early.
S2.feel: Frightened, the kind of fear that has him doing sums in his head at three in the morning.
S2.quote: I'd be sixty in 2028, seven years short of the pension, with four months saved, and no builder's taking on a sixty-year-old improver when a robot works nights for nothing.
S2.fieldNote: This is where the two-year timeline bites: he lands in the gap between losing work and drawing a pension. He worries about his son in the call centre more than himself. His answers turn to public support with no embarrassment, because he sees it as money he paid in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd say we need rules and we need them now, but with five years I'd say it calmer. There'd be time to fight for a proper plan, so I'd be at the meetings, not on the barricades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's different for me with five years. I'd be sixty-three in 2031, and that's close enough that I could maybe bridge the gap with savings, the print works pension, and some odd jobs. It's still tight, but it's a gap I can see across.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the savings hard: every overtime shift Gary can find, and I'd stop the hundred a month and make it two hundred. I'd finish the carpentry course so I can do small repairs for neighbours later. And I'd be at every union meeting pushing for early pension rights for people in my spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but with my hands on the wheel. Five years is enough to steer, if I don't waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut to get to two hundred a month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My pint on Friday with Kwame, for a start, and the football subscription. Asha would say the cigarettes, and she'd be right, I'm down to five a day. That's sixty quid a month on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said odd jobs for neighbours. Would robots not do those too by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but old Mrs Dunne on our road isn't buying a robot to fix her shed door. People round us will still want a man they know. I could be wrong, and I don't really know how cheap they'd get.

S3.say: I'd still say we need rules now, but more calmly. With five years there's time to fight for a proper plan through the union, at meetings rather than on the barricades.
S3.think: Privately five years changes it for me, because I'd be sixty-three in 2031. With savings, the print works pension and odd jobs, I could maybe bridge the gap to the state pension.
S3.do: Doubles monthly savings to two hundred by taking every overtime shift and cutting the pub, football subscription and cigarettes. Finishes the carpentry course for later repair jobs and pushes for early pension rights at the union.
S3.feel: Worried but in control, with enough time to steer if he doesn't waste it.
S3.quote: Old Mrs Dunne on our road isn't buying a robot to fix her shed door. People round us will still want a man they know.
S3.fieldNote: The difference between two and five years is the difference between fear and arithmetic for him. He builds a concrete bridge to his pension, and admits he can't know how cheap robots will get. Cutting cigarettes came up unprompted, which suggests he's serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it fairly, so there's no excuse. If it ends up a mess in 2036, that's a choice the government and the companies made, and I'd keep saying that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, it mostly misses me. I'd be sixty-eight, past the pension age, so my worry is Sam and the grandkids, not me. That's a strange thing to admit, that the slow one is the one I can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with Gary and get properly good at doors and frames, maybe even get to the point I'm not the improver any more. I'd keep saving steady and I'd vote for whoever has a real plan for people being put out of work. And I'd nag Sam to start learning a trade that needs hands, or anything, now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled for myself, but a knot in my stomach for my son. It's the same feeling I had when he left school without a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say to Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, son, you've got ten years, don't do what I did and wait for the letter. Start now, go to night school, learn something. He'd roll his eyes, and then maybe he'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd rather learn the plane than the phone. With ten years, would you try the AI tools after all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe once they're everywhere and I can't avoid it. But I'm not going to be the first, I never am. I'd let Gary show me when he's sick of doing my measuring for me.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do this fairly, so there's no excuse. If 2036 is a mess, it's because the government and companies chose it.
S4.think: Privately this one mostly misses me, because I'd be sixty-eight and past pension age. My worry turns to my son Sam and the grandkids, which is a strange thing to admit.
S4.do: Keeps working at Bramley Build and aims to stop being the improver by mastering doors and frames. Keeps saving at a steady rate, votes for a party with a real plan, and pushes Sam into night school.
S4.feel: Settled for himself, with a knot in his stomach for his son.
S4.quote: Son, you've got ten years, don't do what I did and wait for the letter.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade he moves the worry off himself and onto his son, which shows how much the timeline matters at his age. He still won't be an early adopter of AI tools. The phrase "wait for the letter" ties back to the print works closing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, by 2028, no question. I'd be stuck at sixty with no job and no pension. What would help is being able to take my pension early without losing a big chunk of it, and the union having a deal in place before the robots turn up, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the money. If a robot does my job for nothing, somebody's getting richer off it, and it isn't Gary or me. That's the question nobody on the telly ever asks.

headlineQuote: If a robot does my job for nothing, somebody's getting richer off it, and it isn't Gary or me.
portrait: Nikhil is a fifty-eight-year-old former print worker who started labouring at fifty-five after his newspaper plant closed, and is now a slow but reliable carpenter's improver on a council flat refurbishment. He's a union man who never uses AI tools and would rather learn a hand plane than a phone app. The calm and steady pictures leave him watchful, because he's lost a stable job before. The fast AGI picture alarms him because it strands him at sixty, seven years short of a pension with four months saved, while ten years mostly misses him and turns his worry towards his son.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd be sixty with no job and seven years from his state pension.
whatWouldHelp: Being able to take his pension early without a big cut, and a union deal on retraining and notice agreed before robots arrive.
